table.text: The study received approval from the first author's University's ethics committee (2990, me237).
Following institutional ethics protocols, raw data were destroyed upon study completion, and only aggregated data were retained.
table.header: Analysis of the verbal fluency tasks

table.text: The participants were recruited via the participant recruitment platform Prolific, except for the self-reported AWS who were recruited via Action for Stammering in Children and Stamma.

Based on this approach, we recruited a total of 212 participants (77 neurotypical adults, 68 self-reported dyslexic adults and 67 self-reported AWS) but we removed 11 neurotypical adults due to their not completing the study, stating they used external devices or not following the instructions, while six self-reported dyslexic adults and five self-reported AWS were removed due to failing the manipulation check or using external devices (see the Procedure for details.

Initially, the participants who had been recruited via Prolific were invited to complete demographic information concerning whether they had received a formal diagnosis of dyslexia or diagnosis of any other neurodivergent profiles.
Neurotypical adults were invited to continue Running head: Verbal fluency dyslexia and stuttering if they answered "no" to the Prolific screening question "Literacy difficulties".
If the participants answered "yes" to the Prolific screening question "Literacy difficulties", they were identified as self-reported dyslexic adults.
All the participants were asked to complete two brief screening questionnaires assessing stuttering and dyslexia to support this initial allocation to the different participant groups.
To be included in the self-reported AWS group, the participants were required to have a selfidentified history of developmental stuttering with onset during childhood.
The participants completed explicit compliance and task-integrity instructions prior to beginning the experimental battery.
Before starting the study, the participants were presented with mandatory guidelines emphasizing the scientific necessity of unassisted, natural language processing.

Specifically, at the end of the experiment, the participants completed self-report questions assessing whether they used memory strategies or sought external assistance (e.g., pen and paper, online tools, spell check, or another person).
To encourage honest reporting, the participants were explicitly informed prior to completing these questions that their responses would have no impact on their monetary compensation.

To maintain experimental control in the remote environment, the participants completed a mandatory headphone, bot check, and audio check prior to testing, and tasks were enforced in full-screen browser mode to minimize external distractions.
Prolific and Gorilla allowed us to automatically monitor session completion times and network connectivity to detect and filter out extreme speeders.

The data collection process was overseen by the lead author, who monitored task duration metrics and provided direct participant support via Prolific and email messaging throughout the testing period.
The participants were instructed to think about stuttering severity with an emphasis on overt, or observable, features of stuttering.
Before beginning the experiment, all the participants provided informed consent and completed demographic measures including age, gender, and handedness.
To maintain consistency and control for order effects, all the participants completed the assessments in a fixed, identical order.

The second Running head: Verbal fluency dyslexia and stuttering task, Empty Dots Only, followed the identical rules, but the boxes contained both empty and filled dots, and the participants were instructed to use only the empty dots to form the designs.

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Verbal fluency in dyslexia and stuttering
table.research_questions:
1) we predict that dyslexic adults will show lower phonemic fluency, but not semantic or design fluency than neurotypical adults.

2) we predict that adults who stutter will show lower phonemic fluency, but not semantic or design fluency than neurotypical adults.

3)  At the fine-grained level, dyslexia and stutter diagnosis will predict a smaller number of switches between subcategories on phonemic fluency, while dyslexia and stutter diagnosis will not predict the size of phonemically related clusters of items.

4) We have no clear prediction for whether there will be group differences for dyslexic people and people who stutter in phonemic fluency, switching or clustering.
table.study_type: Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.study_design_overview:
The verbal fluency experiment has a 3 (participant group) within-subject design and a hierarchical design.  Participant groups are neurotypical readers, people who stutter or dyslexic readers.  In addition, we will  use separate hierarchical multiple regression analyses to determine whether the presence of dyslexia or stuttering was a significant predictor of total responses generated, valid responses, number of errors, number of switches, words per cluster and the total number of items generated in each quartile of Letter and Category Fluency. The data for Design Fluency will be analysed in terms of the total number of responses generated, the total valid responses, and the total number of errors.

We will additionally collect individual difference measures relevant to dyslexia. These are: 
phoneme elision, nonword repetition, memory for digits, rapid letter naming and phoneme reversal, spelling, the Gray silent reading task, test of word reading efficiency sight word and phoneme decoding, test of irregular word reading efficiency, author recognition test, Raven's matrices, title recognition test and British Picture vocabulary.
table.randomization: There will be no randomization as the individual differences tests will be conducted in the same order.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to creation of data
table.data_collection_procedures: Participants will be recruited using the Gorilla and Prolific interface. They will also receive reimbursement at a rate equivalent to £11.50 per hour. Non-dyslexic readers must be over 18 years old, with native English as their only proficient language, must not have dyslexia, and have normal/corrected vision. Dyslexic readers will follow the same criteria but must include a formal or a self-diagnosis of dyslexia.
table.sample_size: Our target sample size is 62 neurotypical adults, 62 dyslexic adults and 62 adults who stutter.
table.sample_size_rationale:
Our study aims to investigate differences in phonemic fluency across three distinct groups: dyslexic adults, adults who stutter, and neurotypical adults. As an individual differences study, our primary goal is to compare performance on phonemic fluency tasks between these groups, specifically examining whether dyslexia and stuttering lead to lower scores compared to neurotypical controls, and to what extent these two neurodivergent conditions differ from each other.

To ensure sufficient statistical power to detect meaningful differences, we have opted for a sample size of 62 participants per group, resulting in a total sample size of 186 adults. This decision is informed by an a priori power analysis conducted in an independent t-test.

Based on prior literature and typical effect sizes observed in verbal fluency research involving clinical and neurodevelopmental populations (Lopez- Zamora et al., 2025), the authors had an effect size of d = 2.22 for the main effect of group on phonemic fluency. This choice of effect size is a reasonable balance between detecting subtle but clinically relevant differences and ensuring feasibility given resource constraints.

With an alpha level of α=0.05 (two-tailed) and a desired power of 0.95 (95%), our power analysis indicates that a sample size of approximately 7 per group is required to detect this effect size. However, as previous studies are likely to have overestimated effect sizes, we multiplied it by 2.5 (Simonsohn, 2015) and as we are planning to get individual differences, we aimed to get approximately 62 participants per group is required. This ensures an 95% chance of correctly rejecting the null hypothesis (i.e., detecting a significant difference if one truly exists) and minimizing the risk of a Type II error (false negative).

While time, money, and personnel are always practical considerations in research, our chosen sample size is primarily driven by the need for adequate statistical power to address our research questions effectively. A 2-hour study duration per participant is deemed sufficient to administer the full battery of verbal fluency tasks and other individual difference measures while minimizing participant fatigue.

In summary, the sample size of 62 participants per group is justified by an a priori power analysis aiming to detect a medium effect size in phonemic fluency, ensuring sufficient statistical power to draw meaningful conclusions about the differences between dyslexic, stuttering, and neurotypical adults.
table.stopping_rule: 62 participants per participant group. If participants need to be excluded (e.g. because they fail to complete a task, see Data Exclusion section), they will be replaced to ensure that the final data set has 62 participants per participant group.
table.manipulated_variables:
Phonemic fluency - name or write as many words beginning with a specific phoneme as fast as possible in 60 seconds
Semantic fluency - name or write as many words from a specific category as fast as possible in 60 seconds
Design fluency - complete as many designs as fast as possible in 60 seconds
The individual difference measures:
Author recognition test- select as many correct authors as possible and not select the foils to avoid penalty 
Title recognition test- select as many correct book titles as possible and not select the foils to avoid penalty 
Spelling- you are presented a word, spell them as correctly as possible
British Picture Vocabulary- select the correct word representative of the audio
Gray Silent Reading Test- respond correctly to the comprehension question based on the text
Test of Word Reading Efficiency: Sight word reading- read as many words as possible within 45 seconds.
Test of Word Reading Efficiency: phoneme decoding-read as many pseudowords as possible within 45 seconds.
Test of irregular word reading efficiency: read irregular words
Rapid Letter Naming: name as many letters as possible and time taken (s) is the measure
Nonword repetition-repeat nonwords aloud
Memory for digits- repeat memory aloud
Phoneme elision- hear a word and remove a phoneme (e.g. remove /p/ from spider to make spy). 
Phoneme reversal- hear a nonword and reverse it to make a word (tis becomes sit).
Raven Standard Matrices - select a panel that matches the overarching pattern.

table.statistical_tests:
A general linear mixed model (GLMM) will be used to analyse reaction times and accuracy, using the lme4 package in R. Significance is set at α = 0.05 and if the t values are above 2, the p value is significant (Baayen et al., 2008). The GLMM is conducted on dependent measures, as linear regression coefficients are directly interpretable when interactions or fixed effects are included, making GLMM safer to use. In addition, a linear model will be used as opposed to using a general logistic mixed model since the former produces unbiased estimates of effects on binary outcomes (Gomila, 2020). In the event that we fail to replicate the standard transposed word effect in our initial analysis of the accuracy data, we will re-analyse this data using the type of model that has been used in prior investigations of this phenomenon (i.e. logistic) in order to ensure that the difference between our work and prior studies is not simply due to the use of different statistical approaches.
Statistical analyses will be performed only on the data concerning the ungrammatical sequences, thus the fixed effects are effects of group-sum coded (-1 dyslexia and 1 neurotypical) or (-1 stuttering and 1 neurotypical) and (-1 stuttering and 1 dyslexia). The contrasts conducted on each fixed effect will be sum-coded to make coefficients directly interpretable. In addition, the random effects will include an item and subject intercept with random slopes for condition being included in the random model (see below): accuracy ~ 1 + Component1 * group +(1 |Subject) + (1 group|item). 
In all cases, the maximal random structure model will include the interaction of both conditions with both subjects and items (Barr et al., 2013). A fully random model is used whenever possible.
However, fully specified models often fail to converge. If the model fails to converge, we will simplify the random slopes, removing interactions before main effects in the order of least variance explained until the model converges (Veldre & Andrews, 2014).

The individual differences will be transformed into a composite score if they are highly correlated and placed in a PCA.
table.transformations: The individual differences will be z-transformed to make the measures more likely matched.
table.inference_criteria: We will use the standard p <.05 criteria, using t values must be above 2. In addition, to further assess whether the non-significant effect indeed supports the null hypothesis, we will calculate the Bayes factor, using ‘BayesFactor’ package in R (see Rouder et al., 2012 for details). This result will provide evidence in favour of the null hypothesis. The BF must be below 1/3 to argue in favour of the null hypothesis.
table.data_exclusion_criteria: If a participant fails to complete the experiment, they will not be included in the analysis.  If participants scores at ceiling in memory for digits and they state that they were cheating, their data will be removed from the data set prior to analysis.
table.missing_data_handling: Data partially missing because a participant quit study halfway through will be excluded; if applicable, data partially missing due to unforeseen software errors will be included in the main categorical analyses. However, to ensure we obtain additional observations due to unforeseen software errors, we will use multiple imputation (Woods et al., 2021). In addition, we will investigate any item responses resulting from missing data not at random. For instance, if only 10% of participants respond incorrectly to some items, while a few other items are responded to incorrectly by around 60% of participants, then we will discuss why this may have happened which may lead to additional exploratory analyses (Woods et al., 2021).

Raven -accuracy", "A general linear mixed model (GLMM) will be used to analyse reaction times and accuracy, using the lme4 package in R. Significance is set at α = 0.05 and if the t values are above 2, the p value is significant (Baayen et al., 2008). The GLMM is conducted on dependent measures, as linear regression coefficients are directly interpretable when interactions or fixed effects are included, making GLMM safer to use. In addition, a linear model will be used as opposed to using a general logistic mixed model since the former produces unbiased estimates of effects on binary outcomes (Gomila, 2020). In the event that we fail to replicate the standard transposed word effect in our initial analysis of the accuracy data, we will re-analyse this data using the type of model that has been used in prior investigations of this phenomenon (i.e. logistic) in order to ensure that the difference between our work and prior studies is not simply due to the use of different statistical approaches.
Statistical analyses will be performed only on the data concerning the ungrammatical sequences, thus the fixed effects are effects of group-sum coded (-1 dyslexia and 1 neurotypical) or (-1 stuttering and 1 neurotypical) and (-1 stuttering and 1 dyslexia). The contrasts conducted on each fixed effect will be sum-coded to make coefficients directly interpretable. In addition, the random effects will include an item and subject intercept with random slopes for condition being included in the random model (see below): accuracy ~ 1 + Component1 * group +(1 |Subject) + (1 group|item).
In all cases, the maximal random structure model will include the interaction of both conditions with both subjects and items (Barr et al., 2013). A fully random model is used whenever possible.
However, fully specified models often fail to converge. If the model fails to converge, we will simplify the random slopes, removing interactions before main effects in the order of least variance explained until the model converges (Veldre & Andrews, 2014).

The individual differences will be transformed into a composite score if they are highly correlated and placed in a PCA.", "The individual differences will be z-transformed to make the measures more likely matched.", "We will use the standard p <.05 criteria, using t values must be above 2. This result will provide evidence in favour of the null hypothesis. The BF must be below 1/3 to argue in favour of the null hypothesis.", "If a participant fails to complete the experiment, they will not be included in the analysis. table.text: Independent-samples t-tests on the component scores revealed no significant group differences between any of the paired comparisons: self-reported AWS versus self-reported neurotypical adults (t(122) = -0.01, p = .992), self-reported AWS versus self-reported dyslexic adults (t(122) = -1.32, p = .19), and self-reported dyslexic adults versus neurotypical adults (t(122) = 1.36, p = .18).

Independent-samples t-tests on the component scores revealed no significant group differences between any of the paired comparisons: self-reported AWS versus self-reported neurotypical adults (t(122) = -0.01, p = .992), self-reported AWS versus self-reported dyslexic adults (t(122) = -1.32, p = .19), and self-reported dyslexic adults versus neurotypical adults (t(122) = 1.36, p = .18).

Independent-samples t-tests on the component scores revealed no significant group differences between any of the paired comparisons: self-reported AWS versus self-reported neurotypical adults (t(122) = -0.01, p = .992), self-reported AWS versus self-reported dyslexic adults (t(122) = -1.32, p = .19), and self-reported dyslexic adults versus neurotypical adults (t(122) = 1.36, p = .18).

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 3 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

reproducibility_check.summary_text:
-  We assessed AND ran 6 R code files for reproducibility (each in an isolated Docker container).
-  0 of 6 scripts ran without error when executed.
-  2 referenced inputs unavailable (0 withheld due to size).
-  25 installable dependencies detected.

ethics_statements: The study received approval from the first author's University's ethics committee (2990, me237).
Following institutional ethics protocols, raw data were destroyed upon study completion, and only aggregated data were retained.
live_data_statements: The participants were recruited via the participant recruitment platform Prolific, except for the self-reported AWS who were recruited via Action for Stammering in Children and Stamma.

Based on this approach, we recruited a total of 212 participants (77 neurotypical adults, 68 self-reported dyslexic adults and 67 self-reported AWS) but we removed 11 neurotypical adults due to their not completing the study, stating they used external devices or not following the instructions, while six self-reported dyslexic adults and five self-reported AWS were removed due to failing the manipulation check or using external devices (see the Procedure for details.

Initially, the participants who had been recruited via Prolific were invited to complete demographic information concerning whether they had received a formal diagnosis of dyslexia or diagnosis of any other neurodivergent profiles.
Neurotypical adults were invited to continue Running head: Verbal fluency dyslexia and stuttering if they answered "no" to the Prolific screening question "Literacy difficulties".
If the participants answered "yes" to the Prolific screening question "Literacy difficulties", they were identified as self-reported dyslexic adults.
All the participants were asked to complete two brief screening questionnaires assessing stuttering and dyslexia to support this initial allocation to the different participant groups.
To be included in the self-reported AWS group, the participants were required to have a selfidentified history of developmental stuttering with onset during childhood.
The participants completed explicit compliance and task-integrity instructions prior to beginning the experimental battery.
Before starting the study, the participants were presented with mandatory guidelines emphasizing the scientific necessity of unassisted, natural language processing.

Specifically, at the end of the experiment, the participants completed self-report questions assessing whether they used memory strategies or sought external assistance (e.g., pen and paper, online tools, spell check, or another person).
To encourage honest reporting, the participants were explicitly informed prior to completing these questions that their responses would have no impact on their monetary compensation.

To maintain experimental control in the remote environment, the participants completed a mandatory headphone, bot check, and audio check prior to testing, and tasks were enforced in full-screen browser mode to minimize external distractions.
Prolific and Gorilla allowed us to automatically monitor session completion times and network connectivity to detect and filter out extreme speeders.

The data collection process was overseen by the lead author, who monitored task duration metrics and provided direct participant support via Prolific and email messaging throughout the testing period.
The participants were instructed to think about stuttering severity with an emphasis on overt, or observable, features of stuttering.
Before beginning the experiment, all the participants provided informed consent and completed demographic measures including age, gender, and handedness.
To maintain consistency and control for order effects, all the participants completed the assessments in a fixed, identical order.

The second Running head: Verbal fluency dyslexia and stuttering task, Empty Dots Only, followed the identical rules, but the boxes contained both empty and filled dots, and the participants were instructed to use only the empty dots to form the designs.
The final task, Switching, was based on the same principles, but the participants were asked to alternate between using filled and empty dots within each design.

Given the participant pool size (N = 186), it was necessary to reduce the initial 15 variables to just eight to ensure the reliability of the subsequent Principal Component Analysis (PCA), as it typically requires five to 10 participants per variable (Kass & Tinsley, 1979).

By leveraging remote administration via Prolific and online communication, our study recruited a moderate-powered sample (N = 62 per group) that significantly exceeded those reported in previous work (e.g., Gkalitsiou et al., 2018, N = 32 AWS; Smith-Spark et al., 2017, N = 28 dyslexia).

text.text: Objective: Dyslexia and stuttering are both defined by phonological processing challenges.

Using executive fluency tasks, the current study investigated whether these challenges reflect phonological representations themselves or access to intact representations during selfreported adults who stutter (AWS) and self-reported dyslexic adults.

Method: An online, unsupervised sample of 62 self-reported AWS, 62 self-reported dyslexic adults and 62 neurotypical adults completed a modified, typed version of semantic and phonemic fluency, as well as a mouse-drawn version of design fluency.
We analyzed switching (shifting between subcategories; proxy for retrieval efficiency) and cluster size (words per subcategory, proxy for representational integrity).

Results: Controlling for nonverbal IQ and language measures, hierarchical regression showed that dyslexia and stuttering significantly predicted reduced overall phonemic output, whereas semantic and design fluency remained unaffected.
Both groups showed reduced switching, though more pronounced in the dyslexia group.
Conversely, only stuttering predicted reduced cluster size.
Conclusion: Given the heterogeneity of these neurodivergent profiles, these findings suggest that, in dyslexia, access to phonological representations is affected.
Conversely, stuttering affects the representations themselves.
For individuals presenting these specific cognitive signatures, interventions could be tailored toward either retrieval strategies or representational strengthening.
Developmental dyslexia and developmental stuttering are neurodivergent profiles that have both been linked to challenges with phonological (i.e., speech sound) processing (Elsherif et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Developmental dyslexia and developmental stuttering are neurodivergent profiles that have both been linked to challenges with phonological (i.e., speech sound) processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Elsherif et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: While these neurodivergent groups are often studied in isolation, a direct comparison of their cognitive performance could provide important theoretical insights into the commonalities and differences between them.
Further to this, both neurodivergent profiles tend to be studied predominantly in childhood but are experienced over the lifespan.

While research informing early diagnosis and intervention is clearly very important, there is considerably less understanding of how these profiles manifest themselves in cognition beyond childhood and adolescence and, thus, how adults with these profiles might be best supported.

In tandem with addressing important theoretical issues, samples from adult Running head: Verbal fluency dyslexia and stuttering populations were therefore recruited to the current study as a contribution towards redressing this age-related imbalance in knowledge.

A critical, yet unresolved, question is the extent to which the phonological challenges of both dyslexia and stuttering are compounded or mediated by executive function, a set of higher-order cognitive abilities that includes inhibition, set-shifting, and updating (e.g., Diamond, 2013; Fisk & Sharp, 2004; Miyake et al., 2000).
text.formatted: A critical, yet unresolved, question is the extent to which the phonological challenges of both dyslexia and stuttering are compounded or mediated by executive function, a set of higher-order cognitive abilities that includes inhibition, set-shifting, and updating (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Diamond, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Fisk & Sharp, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">Miyake et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: While previous research has documented executive function differences in both dyslexia (e.g., Brosnan et al., 2002; Smith-Spark et al., 2016; Varvara et al., 2014) and stuttering (Ntourou et al., 2018; Ofoe et al., 2018 Ofoe et al., , 2026;; Treleaven & Coalson, 2020), the relationship between these executive processes and phonological performance remains debated.
text.formatted: While previous research has documented executive function differences in both dyslexia (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Brosnan et al., 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b132">Smith-Spark et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b152">Varvara et al., 2014)</ref> and stuttering <ref type="bibr" target="#b95">(Ntourou et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">Ofoe et al., 2018</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">Ofoe et al., , 2026;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b147">Treleaven & Coalson, 2020)</ref>, the relationship between these executive processes and phonological performance remains debated.

text.text: The research reported in the current paper, therefore, investigated verbal and nonverbal executive fluency in self-reported dyslexic adults, self-reported adults who stutter (AWS) 1 , and neurotypical adults.

The overall aim of this study was to evaluate three competing theoretical accounts by examining how domain-general executive functioning interacts with both the quality of phonological representations and the mechanisms of phonological access.
By contrasting these dynamics across dyslexia and stuttering, we sought to clarify whether observed difficulties are due to storage, retrieval, or a domain-general executive constraint.

Neurocognitive Profiles: Dyslexia, Stuttering, and Executive Function Developmental Dyslexia is a neurodivergent profile manifesting in approximately seven to 10% of the population (e.g., Peterson & Pennington, 2012).
text.formatted: Neurocognitive Profiles: Dyslexia, Stuttering, and Executive Function Developmental Dyslexia is a neurodivergent profile manifesting in approximately seven to 10% of the population (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">Peterson & Pennington, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, developmental stuttering is a complex neurodevelopmental condition affecting approximately 8.5% of the paediatric population and 0.81% of adults (Yairi & Ambrose, 2013).

text.text: It is characterised by a disruption to the motor planning necessary for speech (Smith & Weber, 2017).

text.text: Like dyslexia, models conceptualize stuttering within multifactorial frameworks (e.g., Smith & Weber, 2017), wherein speech disruptions emerge from the interplay of neural, speech-motor, linguistic, emotional, and cognitive variables (Bowers et al., 2018).

text.text: Both children who stutter (CWS) and AWS frequently demonstrate challenges with executive function, particularly when inhibitory control and cognitive flexibility are required (Anderson & Ofoe, 2019; Eggers et al., 2012 Eggers et al., , 2013;; Eichorn et al., 2018; Kakuta & Kawasaki, 2025; Lescht et al., 2022).

text.text: These executive function differences may create a dynamic feedback loop: managing complex cognitive loads can tax executive resources heavily during speech production, while the ongoing energy expenditure required to navigate a non-fluent speech system can, in turn, deplete those available executive resources (Anderson & Ofoe, 2019; Eggers et al., 2012; Eichorn et al., 2018; Kakuta & Kawasaki, 2025; Lescht et al., 2022).

text.text: It remains strongly debated whether these cognitive variations reflect generalized cognitive challenges or domain-specific language constraints (Bahrami et al., 2014; Lescht et al., 2022).

text.text: Although dyslexia and stuttering present distinct language processing profiles, research suggests the two conditions are not mutually exclusive. Elsherif et al. (2021) identified a significant co-occurrence rate of 30-40%, an overlap which far exceeds what would be expected by chance.

(2021)</ref> identified a significant co-occurrence rate of 30-40%, an overlap which far exceeds what would be expected by chance.

text.text: By evaluating individual differences across orthographic, phonological, and semantic domains, these authors sought to isolate the source of this co-occurrence.
The authors found that the two neurodivergent groups showed similar scores in measures related to phonological processing (see also Elsherif et al., 2025).

text.text: Because of this comparability, it is difficult to determine whether a shared core difference in both phonological processing and executive function abilities affects the two neurodivergent groups.

Within a contemporary multifactorial framework (McGrath et al., 2021; Smith & Weber, 2017), converging profiles raise a critical question as to whether these shared behavioural outcomes stem from a common phonological origin, overlapping executive demands or distinct interacting cognitive mechanisms.

text.text: Answering this question is critical for refining the diagnostic and the theoretical boundaries between dyslexia and stutter.
Theoretical accounts of the phonological difficulties in dyslexia are generally divided between two primary perspectives.

The manifestation of dyslexia traits is heavily modulated by crosslinguistic factors such as orthographic transparency, which modulates the mapping of phonological representations to written symbols (see Yael et al., 2015; Ziegler & Goswami, 2005).
text.formatted: The manifestation of dyslexia traits is heavily modulated by crosslinguistic factors such as orthographic transparency, which modulates the mapping of phonological representations to written symbols (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b158">Yael et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b161">Ziegler & Goswami, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: The prevailing degraded representation hypothesis suggests that phonological representations themselves are less robust and distinct in dyslexic individuals (Leong et al., 2011; Ziegler & Goswami, 2005).
text.formatted: The prevailing degraded representation hypothesis suggests that phonological representations themselves are less robust and distinct in dyslexic individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">(Leong et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b161">Ziegler & Goswami, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: These degraded representations then disrupt higher-level processing and reading development, particularly in opaque orthographies such as English.

An alternative perspective, the delayed phonological access hypothesis (Ramus & Szenkovits, 2008), posits that phonological representations remain intact but are difficult to retrieve under specific cognitive pressures.
text.formatted: An alternative perspective, the delayed phonological access hypothesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b116">(Ramus & Szenkovits, 2008)</ref>, posits that phonological representations remain intact but are difficult to retrieve under specific cognitive pressures.

text.text: This account suggests that the challenges become most apparent during tasks that require the explicit manipulation of speech sounds, speeded Running head: Verbal fluency dyslexia and stuttering retrieval or short-term memory, meaning that dyslexic traits may be exacerbated by high task demands.

This explanation has been supported empirically (e.g., Boets et al., 2013; Dickie et al., 2013; Ramus et al., 2013; Szenkovits et al., 2016) and the data reported in the adult dyslexia literature largely align with this account.

text.text: Given that many AWS exhibit phonological processing challenges (e.g., Elsherif et al., 2021; Pelczarski & Yaruss, 2014), the theoretical framework of the degraded phonological representation hypothesis (e.g., Leong et al., 2011) and the delayed phonological access hypothesis (e.g., Ramus & Szenkovits, 2008) provide a useful lens for investigating the underlying phonological processing mechanisms in this neurodivergence too.

text.text: As noted previously, a representational account (Ziegler & Goswami, 2005) posits that the underlying phonological units themselves are structurally unstable or incomplete, while an access-based account suggests that internal phonological representations remain intact but become disrupted during real-time, time-pressured retrieval.

text.text: The EXPLAN theory (Howell & Au-Yeung, 2002) directly aligns with the latter phonological access framework, proposing that stuttering arises from a temporal processing mismatch between linguistic planning and motor execution.

text.text: Under the EXPLAN model, when motor execution outpaces linguistic planning, speakers either stall execution (repeating planned words or pausing) or advance into partially encoded plans (Ning et al., 2017).

text.text: Evaluating these competing representational and access mechanisms within a transparent multifactorial framework can help to clarify whether the overlapping behavioral profiles found in dyslexia and stuttering reflect shared transdiagnostic mechanisms or distinct cognitive pathways.
In the current study, performance on executive fluency tasks was used to directly investigate this issue.
Verbal fluency requires the generation of non-repeating items under time limits, typically 60 seconds, and following specific rules (Villalobos et al., 2022 (Villalobos et al., , 2023)).
text.formatted: Verbal fluency requires the generation of non-repeating items under time limits, typically 60 seconds, and following specific rules <ref type="bibr" target="#b154">(Villalobos et al., 2022</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b155">(Villalobos et al., , 2023))</ref>.

text.text: The most frequently administered verbal fluency tasks are phonemic fluency, where participants produce words starting with a specific letter while avoiding proper nouns, repetitions, plurals or names (e.g., Benton, 1968; Borkowski et al., 1967), and semantic fluency (generating items from a specific category) (Newcombe, 1969).

text.text: Verbal fluency performance can be measured with coarse-grained markers (e.g., total number of items produced or correct number items generated) and finer-grained indices (e.g., cluster size and number of switches) (e.g., Dorchies et al., 2024; Troyer et al., 1997).

text.text: Clustering typically reflects the number of closely related items generated in succession.
Clustering is driven by automatic spreading of activation between conceptually or phonologically related words (Rosen & Engle, 1997).
text.formatted: Clustering is driven by automatic spreading of activation between conceptually or phonologically related words <ref type="bibr" target="#b122">(Rosen & Engle, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: For example, after producing the word "fat", a participant may list other words such as 'fan', 'far' and 'fad' or apples, a participant may list other fruits that grow on trees such as 'pears', 'peaches' and 'plums'.

Such related items are usually produced in spurts or in temporal clusters that have short intervals between items (e.g., Bousfield & Sedgewick, 1944; Henry & Crawford, 2004; Henry et al., 2015; Troyer et al., 1997).
text.formatted: Such related items are usually produced in spurts or in temporal clusters that have short intervals between items (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Bousfield & Sedgewick, 1944;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Henry & Crawford, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Henry et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b149">Troyer et al., 1997)</ref>.

text.text: These related items are generated until no more words belonging to that subcategory are available, at which point the individual initiates a search for a new subcategory from which to continue producing items.
Switching involves cognitive flexibility in transitioning efficiently between distinct subcategories to guide retrieval (Troyer et al., 1997).
text.formatted: Switching involves cognitive flexibility in transitioning efficiently between distinct subcategories to guide retrieval <ref type="bibr" target="#b149">(Troyer et al., 1997)</ref>.

text.text: For example, after listing all the words that they know beginning with "fa", participants may utter "fit", "fund" and "foot" or may decide to switch from arboreal fruits to vine-growing fruits such as "grapes", "tomatoes".
Switching is a cognitively effortful process that requires roles for strategic search, cognitive flexibility and cognitive control (Mayr, 2002; Troyer, 2000; Troyer et al., 1997).

text.text: Verbal fluency demands an interplay of language abilities and domain-general skills, including attention, memory, processing speed, and inhibitory control, reflecting both unity and diversity in retrieval processes (e.g., Dorchies et al., 2024; Gustavson et al., 2019; Schmidt et al., 2017; Shao et al., 2014).

text.text: Verbal fluency has been well studied in dyslexic populations (see Smith-Spark et al., 2017, for an overview).

text.text: Broadly speaking, dyslexia-related phonemic fluency differences are well established (e.g., López-Zamora et al., 2025; Mengsidiou & Marshall, 2019; Shareef et al., 2019; Smith-Spark et al., 2017), while the effect of dyslexia on semantic fluency tasks is less clear cut.

text.text: Some studies indicate group differences in semantic fluency (e.g., López-Zamora et al., 2025; Shareef et al., 2019), while others do not (e.g., Mengsidiou & Marshall, 2019).

text.text: To our knowledge, the vast majority of these studies have focused on overall output measures and very few studies have reported average cluster size and switching in dyslexic individuals.

One study report that dyslexic adolescents do not differ in the number of clusters, the number of switches or the size of clusters relative to neurotypical adolescents (e.g., Mielnik et al., 2015), while other studies have found that dyslexic adults showed lower scores only for phonemic switching compared with neurotypical adults (Mengsidiou & Marshall, 2019; Smith-Spark et al., 2017).

text.text: Research on verbal fluency in AWS is considerably more limited.
However, extant work consistently shows phonemic fluency difficulties alongside preserved semantic fluency across spoken and typed modalities (Bahrami et al., 2014; Lescht et al., 2022).

text.text: Expanding upon this work, Gkalitsiou and Werle (2026) replicated these findings and took the research a step further by analyzing fine-grained measures of verbal fluency.

text.text: They found that, while AWS and controls showed similar levels of clustering, AWS exhibited fewer phonemic switches.

While valuable insights into lexical and executive performance have been obtained from these studies, it is important to note that verbal fluency measures evaluate the constrained lexical retrieval of isolated words rather than the real-time speech-motor execution dynamics that are characteristic of connected speech in which stuttering typically manifests (Howell & Au-Yeung, 2002).
text.formatted: While valuable insights into lexical and executive performance have been obtained from these studies, it is important to note that verbal fluency measures evaluate the constrained lexical retrieval of isolated words rather than the real-time speech-motor execution dynamics that are characteristic of connected speech in which stuttering typically manifests <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Howell & Au-Yeung, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, it remains unclear whether these switching variations reflect a localized phonological phenomenon or a broader executive function challenge.

To address this issue, and to isolate executive function from phonological processing, researchers can use nonverbal alternatives to the phonemic and semantic fluency tasks, such as design fluency tasks (Ruff et al., 1987).
text.formatted: To address this issue, and to isolate executive function from phonological processing, researchers can use nonverbal alternatives to the phonemic and semantic fluency tasks, such as design fluency tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b123">(Ruff et al., 1987)</ref>.

text.text: Design fluency requires participants to connect printed dots with straight lines to generate novel patterns within a set time limit.

Such tasks assess visuospatial executive skills (Mengisidou & Marshall, 2019) without relying on phonological representations and thus provide an index of domain-general executive control (Chen et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Such tasks assess visuospatial executive skills <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">(Mengisidou & Marshall, 2019)</ref> without relying on phonological representations and thus provide an index of domain-general executive control <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Chen et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Both self-reported dyslexic adults and self-reported AWS would be predicted to show similar levels of performance to neurotypical adults in design fluency, since visuospatial executive skills remain distinct from linguistic processing.
However, despite its utility in mapping cognitive profiles, research on design fluency in dyslexia remains both sparse and mixed.

Some studies report performance differences (e.g., Reiter et al., 2005), while others find no dyslexia-related group differences (e.g., Griffiths, 1991; Mengisidou & Marshall, 2019; Smith-Spark et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Some studies report performance differences (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b118">Reiter et al., 2005)</ref>, while others find no dyslexia-related group differences (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Griffiths, 1991;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">Mengisidou & Marshall, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b133">Smith-Spark et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: There is even less clarity in the case of stuttering with, to the best of our knowledge, no published studies investigating design fluency.

Therefore, the current literature relating to executive fluency in stuttering and dyslexia highlights a central yet unexplored theoretical tension as to whether the challenges in executive fluency reflect poor phonological representations (that limit the pool of available items or an impoverished lexical storage) or delayed phonological access (where intact representations are harder to retrieve under timed conditions or an executive failure to navigate the network efficiently).

To address this important theoretical point, the current study examined whether lower total executive fluency outputs are driven by the size of retrieved clusters or the efficiency of the search process itself, isolating cluster size from switching, to test whether different neurodivergent profiles share a common mechanical failure in lexical navigation.

Furthermore, by providing a fine-grained comparison of the performance of self-reported AWS and selfreported dyslexic adults, the current study also investigated whether their phonemic fluency challenges reflect a shared executive-phonological difficulty or distinct underlying cognitive mechanisms.
Finally, by using a non-verbal design fluency task, it could be determined whether the challenges in dyslexia and stuttering stem from phonological or executive function challenges.

Guided by the Lexical Quality Hypothesis (LQH; Perfetti, 1992 Perfetti, , 2007 Perfetti, , 2017;; Perfetti & Hart, 2001 , 2002), which posits that lexical retrieval depends on precision (the specificity and detail of individual representations) and redundancy (the strength of binding across orthographic, phonological, and semantic codes), we incorporated individual-difference measures of language and literacy skills (see Elsherif et al., 2022 Elsherif et al., , 2023 Elsherif et al., , 2025) ) and conducted a Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on orthographic, phonological, and semantic measures to derive latent dimensions of language skill (Acheson et al., 2008).

text.text: Taking this approach allowed us to test predictions based on three different theories, namely phonological access (Ramus & Szenkovits, 2008), the degraded phonological representation hypothesis (Ziegler & Goswami, 2005) and an explanation based on domain-general executive difficulties (e.g., Smith-Spark & Fisk, 2007).
text.formatted: Taking this approach allowed us to test predictions based on three different theories, namely phonological access <ref type="bibr" target="#b116">(Ramus & Szenkovits, 2008)</ref>, the degraded phonological representation hypothesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b161">(Ziegler & Goswami, 2005</ref>) and an explanation based on domain-general executive difficulties (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b130">Smith-Spark & Fisk, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: If executive fluency challenges stem directly from imprecise or noisy phonological representations, then it would be predicted that self-reported dyslexic adults and self-reported AWS would produce smaller cluster sizes in phonemic fluency, while switching frequency and performance on semantic and design fluency would remain comparable to controls.
This pattern would be expected by the degraded phonological representation account hypothesis (Ziegler & Goswami, 2005).
text.formatted: This pattern would be expected by the degraded phonological representation account hypothesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b161">(Ziegler & Goswami, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Instead, if representations are intact but access and language-bound executive regulation (e.g., competitor suppression during retrieval) are inefficient, both neurodivergent groups would show a reduced number of switches across verbal tasks (phonemic and semantic fluency), while showing normal cluster sizes and unimpaired design fluency.

Based on the prior literature and the typical effect sizes reported in verbal fluency research involving neurodivergent participants (e.g., Lopez-Zamora et al., 2025), an effect size of d = 2.22 was decided upon for the main effect of the participant group on phonemic fluency.

text.text: This choice of effect size strikes a reasonable balance between detecting subtle but clinically relevant differences and ensuring feasibility given resource constraints.

With an alpha level set at α = 0.05 (two-tailed) and a desired power of 0.95 (95%), our power analysis indicated that a sample size of approximately seven per group was required to detect this effect size.
To reduce M-Error (Gelman & Carlin, 2014), we applied a 2.5x multiplier to previous sample sizes (Simonsohn, 2015) as an initial step.

text.text: However, to account for the added complexity of measuring standardized measures of spelling, reading fluency, phonology, vocabulary and reading comprehension, we further adjusted our target to 62 participants per group.
This ensured that we had a 95% chance of correctly rejecting the null hypothesis and reduced the risk of Type II error.
In addition, this sample size was in line with or larger than other published studies examining verbal fluency in either dyslexia or stuttering (Lescht et al., 2022; Smith-Spark et al., 2017).

text.text: The participants were recruited via the participant recruitment platform Prolific, except for the self-reported AWS who were recruited via Action for Stammering in Children and Stamma.
Individuals were eligible to take part if they were aged between 18 and 36 years and spoke English as their first language.

Based on this approach, we recruited a total of 212 participants (77 neurotypical adults, 68 self-reported dyslexic adults and 67 self-reported AWS) but we removed 11 neurotypical adults due to their not completing the study, stating they used external devices or not following the instructions, while six self-reported dyslexic adults and five self-reported AWS were removed due to failing the manipulation check or using external devices (see the Procedure for details.

After removing these participants, we had a final validated sample of 186 British-educated native English participants (62 neurotypical adults, aged 19-36 years (age M = 29.5 years, SD = 4.5, 31 women), 62 self-reported dyslexic adults, aged 20-36 years, (age M = 28.4 years, SD = 4.81, 32 women), and 62 self-reported AWS, aged 20-36 years (age M = 28.2 years, SD = 4.31, 31 women).

Education level was recorded as their highest completed academic qualification and was categorized numerically as follows: UK A-levels (coded as 1), Bachelor's degree (coded as 2), Master's degree (coded as 3) and PhD (coded as 4).

text.text: The participants completed explicit compliance and task-integrity instructions prior to beginning the experimental battery.
Before starting the study, the participants were presented with mandatory guidelines emphasizing the scientific necessity of unassisted, natural language processing.

Specifically, at the end of the experiment, the participants completed self-report questions assessing whether they used memory strategies or sought external assistance (e.g., pen and paper, online tools, spell check, or another person).
To encourage honest reporting, the participants were explicitly informed prior to completing these questions that their responses would have no impact on their monetary compensation.
Responses to these checks were screened to identify and exclude data from the participants who relied on unauthorized external aids.

To maintain experimental control in the remote environment, the participants completed a mandatory headphone, bot check, and audio check prior to testing, and tasks were enforced in full-screen browser mode to minimize external distractions.
Platform-level controls monitored network connectivity and strictly prevented browser tab switching during task completion.
Prolific and Gorilla allowed us to automatically monitor session completion times and network connectivity to detect and filter out extreme speeders.

Completion times were continuously tracked, and trials or participant sessions with impossibly fast keypress latencies, completing the experiment in one hour for a two hour experiment, severe timing artifacts, including >3SD from the sample median battery completion time, indicating multi-tasking or task desertion, severe network disruptions or connectivity disruptions were identified and excluded prior to analysis.

text.text: Procedure Manipulation checks.
Before beginning the experiment, all the participants provided informed consent and completed demographic measures including age, gender, and handedness.
To ensure data integrity and participant authenticity, a multi-stage verification protocol was implemented.

This was designed to differentiate between the two target cohorts: self-reported AWS and self-reported dyslexic adults, while excluding automated bot responses or "bad faith" participants attempting to access the study's compensation.
This verification was conducted in the form of a phenomenological manipulation check requiring the participants to describe the internal mechanisms of their neurodivergent profile.

For the self-reported AWS, the check focused on pre-phonatory physical tension and the cognitive decision-making involved in word substitution ("What words or phrases come to mind when you think about blocks?").
For the self-reported dyslexic adults, the verification probe targeted orthographic retrieval.

The participants described the internal cognitive strategies used when phonetic-tographemic mapping fails ("What words or phrases come to mind when you try to see the word or hear the sounds and when it becomes blurry?").
Responses were screened for processoriented markers such as sub-vocalizing to bridge phonetic gaps.
These indicators served to Running head: Verbal fluency dyslexia and stuttering distinguish authentic lived experience from superficial or 'textbook' knowledge of the neurodivergent profiles.
The overall study required each participant to attend a single session remotely, which lasted approximately two hours.
To maintain consistency and control for order effects, all the participants completed the assessments in a fixed, identical order.
The study was conducted without direct participant-examiner supervision; however, the protocol was standardized to minimize variability.

The selection of these measures was guided by the Lexical Quality Hypothesis (Perfetti, 2007), which posits that high-quality lexical representations are formed through the integrated precision of orthographic, phonological, and semantic constituents (detailed further in Table 1).

text.text: These domains included non-verbal intelligence and measures grouped into four main areas.
A comprehensive battery of standardized tests was used to assess four core cognitive-linguistic domains: Orthography, Phonology, Reading Fluency, and Semantics.

The first area was orthographic processing, which included three measures: spelling dictation, an author recognition test, and a title recognition test (see Elsherif et al., 2022 Elsherif et al., , 2023 Elsherif et al., , 2025, for further details).
text.formatted: The first area was orthographic processing, which included three measures: spelling dictation, an author recognition test, and a title recognition test (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Elsherif et al., 2022</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Elsherif et al., , 2023</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Elsherif et al., , 2025</ref>, for further details).

text.text: The second area, phonological processing, involved four tests: phoneme elision, phoneme reversal, nonword repetition, and memory for digits.
The third area, reading fluency, was assessed with four tests: regular word reading, irregular word reading, pseudoword reading, and rapid letter naming.
Finally, the fourth area, semantic processing, included two tests: receptive vocabulary, and a reading comprehension test.
To ensure the accuracy of data collection, the modality of response was tailored to the specific cognitive task.
All orthographic, phonological processing and semantic processing tasks were administered via a typing interface, allowing the participants to record their responses directly.
Only tasks inherently requiring oral production, specifically reading fluency measures, such as TOWRE, TIWRE and rapid letter naming, were conducted orally.

text.text: The participants performed a series of 60second verbal fluency trials.

The first task was Phonemic Fluency, where the participants typed as many distinct words as possible beginning with a specified letter (F, A, or S), while strictly excluding numbers, places or proper names.
The second task, Semantic Fluency, required generating words belonging to a specific semantic category, the names of animals.
The third task was Category Switching, where the participants alternated quickly between two different semantic categories, fruits and furniture, for 60 seconds.

All responses were typed instead of spoken (to accommodate potential articulatory differences for AWS), a choice of response modality supported by Lescht et al. (2022), who have argued that the phonological challenges for AWS are not affected by the response output.
text.formatted: All responses were typed instead of spoken (to accommodate potential articulatory differences for AWS), a choice of response modality supported by <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Lescht et al. (2022)</ref>, who have argued that the phonological challenges for AWS are not affected by the response output.

text.text: Three tasks from the D-KEFS Design Fluency subtest, adapted for digital administration, were also presented to the participants.
Using a computer mouse, the participants drew designs within a booklet-style interface featuring rows of boxes, each containing an array of dots.
The first task, Filled Dots, required the participants to connect dots using exactly four non-isolated straight lines to create as many unique designs as possible within 60 seconds.

The second Running head: Verbal fluency dyslexia and stuttering task, Empty Dots Only, followed the identical rules, but the boxes contained both empty and filled dots, and the participants were instructed to use only the empty dots to form the designs.
Performance on these two tasks was later combined for scoring.
The final task, Switching, was based on the same principles, but the participants were asked to alternate between using filled and empty dots within each design.
Following the completion of all tasks, the participants received a written debriefing.
To understand group differences (specifically between self-reported AWS and self-reported dyslexic adults), we performed an independent-samples t-test for each standardized test (see Table 2).

text.text: All statistical analyses were conducted using R (version 4.5.2), with a significance level (alpha) set at 0.05 (two-tailed).
Key packages used were 'tidyverse' for data handling and 'effsize' for calculating effect sizes (Cohen's d).
To control for Type I error in unplanned comparisons, a Holm-Bonferroni correction was applied to the reported p-values.

To transparently illustrate both individual-level variability and group-level distribution, we created multi-panel raincloud plots for each cognitive and language measure, plus significant effects for phonemic and semantic fluency measures.

Each plot integrates: (1) jittered raw data points reflecting individual participant scores, (2) centralized boxplots displaying group medians and interquartile ranges, and (3) probability density slabs to show the overall shape and density of distribution for each group (NT, PWD, and PWS).

text.text: To prepare the data, scores from the individual cognitive measures were z-transformed using the scale() function in R to make the measures more comparable.
Next, Pearson's productmoment correlations (r) were calculated to confirm that the measures intended for grouping were sufficiently intercorrelated.

This confirmation of strong intercorrelation (e.g., nonword repetition and memory for digits reflecting phonological short-term memory; Wagner et al., 1999) validated the assumption that these measures reflected a single underlying construct.

text.text: The z-scores were computed via scaling and the centre function in R. These related measures were then averaged to create composite scores.
This averaging process reduced the overall number of variables entered into the PCA, while also ensuring that the combined score represented a unified construct rather than disparate measures.

Prior to conducting the Principal Component Analysis (PCA), we evaluated the suitability of the dataset for dimensionality reduction using the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) measure of sampling adequacy and Bartlett's test of sphericity.
A KMO value exceeding .5 (Field, 2009) and a significant result in Bartlett's test (p < .001) were established as the criteria for determining appropriateness.
text.formatted: A KMO value exceeding .5 <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Field, 2009)</ref> and a significant result in Bartlett's test (p < .001) were established as the criteria for determining appropriateness.

text.text: Following these checks, PCA was performed in which the individual difference measures and the newly created composite scores were entered.
This statistical technique identifies underlying factors (components) that explain most of the variability in the data.
Both varimax (orthogonal) and oblique rotations were used to facilitate the interpretation of factor loadings, using the GPArotation package (Bernaards & Jennrich, 2005) in R (R Core Team, 2017).

text.text: There are varying approaches to quantifying cluster size.
Traditionally, size is calculated by counting from the second word in a sequence (the n-1 method; see Mayr, 2002), which results in single words having a cluster size of zero.

text.text: However, following the recommendations of Henry et al. (2015) and Smith-Spark et al. (2017) to avoid skewed data, we adopted the n method.

text.text: Under this approach, every word is accounted for: single words that do not share a semantic or phonemic link with preceding or subsequent items are treated as distinct clusters of size one, while multi-word groupings are scored based on the total number of words they contain.
Finally, the Switching trials (for both Semantic and Phonemic Fluency) were assessed based on the total number of correct responses and the total number of correct switching responses.
Due to the nature of the responses made on the Design Fluency task, analyses were restricted to three measures, total responses, valid responses, and errors.
In addition, category switching and design switching were assessed based on the total number of correct switching responses.
The fine-grained analyses of phonemic and semantic fluency (i.e., switching and clustering) were conducted by the first author (MME), who has training in these metrics.
Standardized scoring criteria were followed throughout.
To ensure scoring consistency, a preliminary review of 10% of the dataset was independently evaluated by a research assistant, demonstrating high inter-rater reliability with 95% agreement.
Following institutional ethics protocols, raw data were destroyed upon study completion, and only aggregated data were retained.

We selected hierarchical multiple regression as our primary analytical framework to assess the incremental predictive power of group membership (dyslexia and stuttering) after controlling for non-verbal IQ and broader cognitive domains.

Separate hierarchical multiple regression analyses were used to determine whether the presence of dyslexia or stuttering For the hierarchical regression, a group factor (sum coded with AWS as the intercept) was entered as a fixed effect.

The two components identified from the PCA analysis (lexical and phonological precision) were included as additional fixed effects in the model and were analyzed as continuous variables to maximize statistical power and precision.
In instances where interaction terms reached statistical significance, we performed post-hoc visualization to interpret the directionality and nature of the effects.
For these visualizations only, we categorized continuous PCA data into 'high' and 'low' groups via a median split, ensuring balanced group sizes.
This approach was used solely as a diagnostic aid to plot interaction patterns and clarify the relationship between cognitive domains and fluency performance across groups.
It did not inform the primary hypothesis testing, which relied entirely on continuous data.
All comparisons were performed using two-tailed tests with the conventional p <.05 threshold for statistical significance (ɑ).

To address task impurity issues and collinearity among individual neuropsychological measures, theoretically driven composite scores (Z-scored) were created for memory, reading fluency, and print exposure prior to dimensionality reduction (see Supplementary Materials for the full correlation matrix and composite construction details).

A Principal Component Analysis (PCA) with oblimin rotation was then conducted on these composites and the remaining individual measures to extract underlying cognitive constructs (see Supplementary Materials for full PCA parameters, factor loadings, and KMO/Bartlett's statistics).

Two primary components emerged, accounting for 53% of the variance: Lexical Precision (comprising receptive vocabulary, print exposure, irregular word reading, and comprehension) and Phonological Precision (comprising reading fluency, phonological awareness, phoneme reversal, short-term memory, and spelling).

Independent-samples t-tests on the component scores revealed no significant group differences between any of the paired comparisons: self-reported AWS versus self-reported neurotypical adults (t(122) = -0.01, p = .992), self-reported AWS versus self-reported dyslexic adults (t(122) = -1.32, p = .19), and self-reported dyslexic adults versus neurotypical adults (t(122) = 1.36, p = .18).

For Phonological Precision, the neurotypical adults scored significantly higher than both the self-reported AWS (t(122) = 6.81, p < .001) and the self-reported dyslexic adults (t(122) = 7.38, p < .001), with no significant difference being found between the self-reported AWS and the self-reported dyslexic adults (t(122) = -0.35, p = .73).

The primary objective of the current study was to differentiate between the theoretical accounts of the phonological challenges experienced in dyslexia and stuttering.
We adopted a staged analytical approach in which we first established broad cognitive indices via PCA before then seeing how these indices related to executive fluency performance.

The PCA distilled individual differences into lexical precision (vocabulary and print exposure) and phonological precision (short-term memory, phonological awareness, and retrieval; Elsherif et al., 2025).
text.formatted: The PCA distilled individual differences into lexical precision (vocabulary and print exposure) and phonological precision (short-term memory, phonological awareness, and retrieval; <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Elsherif et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Our individual differences results aligned with previous findings (e.g., Elsherif et al., 2021; see also Coalson & Byrd, 2015; Pelczarski & Yaruss, 2014; Spencer & Weber-Fox, 2014 for stuttering; Snowling, 2019; Smith-Spark et al., 2017, for dyslexia), suggesting that the self-reported AWS and the self-reported dyslexic adults show overlapping phonological processing profiles.

text.text: Furthermore, both self-reported neurodivergent groups performed below the level of neurotypical adults on the TOWRE, a pattern consistent with shared challenge in rapid phonological decoding.

This extensive overlap in self-reported cooccurring neurodivergent traits, including the proportion of self-reported AWS scoring within the mild dyslexia range and the notable reported history of childhood stuttering within the dyslexia group, highlights a shared challenge rooted in phonological processing that appears to cross clinical boundaries.
However, these shared features coexist with clear behavioral dissociations.
The self-reported dyslexic group showed uniquely poor spelling performance on the British Ability Scales (Elliott et al., 1996).

text.text: Furthermore, on the TIWRE (Reynolds et al., 2007), self-reported dyslexic adults performed significantly below neurotypical controls, whereas the performance of AWS fell between these two groups.
text.formatted: Furthermore, on the TIWRE <ref type="bibr" target="#b119">(Reynolds et al., 2007)</ref>, self-reported dyslexic adults performed significantly below neurotypical controls, whereas the performance of AWS fell between these two groups.

text.text: Having established the underlying cognitive factors (lexical precision and phonological precision) via the PCA, we then compared the verbal fluency measures against non-verbal design fluency indices to provide a novel, granular dissociation between the two neurodivergent profiles.
Phonemic fluency was assessed using a composite score derived from performance in response to three initial phonemes ('F', 'A', and 'S').

For all three participant groups, the volume of both total and valid responses generated was primarily influenced by phonological precision, lexical precision, and dyslexia, stuttering, or both neurodivergent profiles.

Our finding that the self-reported AWS and the self-reported dyslexic adults generated fewer correct items than the neurotypical controls aligns with an extensive body of literature that consistently documents phonemic fluency difficulties in English (e.g., Brosnan et al., 2002; Smith-Spark et al., 2017; Snowling et al., 1997) and other orthographies, including French (Plaza et al., 2002), Greek (Mengisidiou & Marshall, 2019), German (Landerl et al., 2009), Italian (Varvara et al., 2014), and Portuguese (Moura et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Our finding that the self-reported AWS and the self-reported dyslexic adults generated fewer correct items than the neurotypical controls aligns with an extensive body of literature that consistently documents phonemic fluency difficulties in English (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Brosnan et al., 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b133">Smith-Spark et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b135">Snowling et al., 1997)</ref> and other orthographies, including French <ref type="bibr" target="#b112">(Plaza et al., 2002)</ref>, <ref type="bibr">Greek (Mengisidiou & Marshall, 2019)</ref>, German <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Landerl et al., 2009)</ref>, Italian <ref type="bibr" target="#b152">(Varvara et al., 2014)</ref>, and Portuguese <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">(Moura et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, reduced phonemic fluency output has been observed in both children (Bahrami et al., 2014) and adults (Gkalitsiou & Werle, 2026; Lescht et al., 2022) who stutter.

text.text: On the phonemic fluency task, the self-reported dyslexic adults also produced significantly fewer switches than the neurotypical adults and the self-reported AWS, but the self-reported dyslexic and neurotypical adults did not differ in average cluster size.

The lack of a relationship between self-reported dyslexia and cluster size in the current study is consistent with the previous literature, using verified diagnoses (Mielnik et al., 2015; Smith-Spark et al., 2017).
text.formatted: The lack of a relationship between self-reported dyslexia and cluster size in the current study is consistent with the previous literature, using verified diagnoses <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">(Mielnik et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b133">Smith-Spark et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, the self-reported AWS scored lower in average cluster size than the neurotypical adults and the self-reported dyslexic adults, with the self-reported AWS showing fewer switches than neurotypical adults but significantly more than the self-reported dyslexic group.

While evidence at this fine-grained measurement level remains sparse in the literature on executive fluency in stuttering, our findings are not consistent with previous research where no group difference in clustering was reported (Gkalitsiou & Werle, 2026).
