text.text: One explanation for this discrepancy relates to differing choices of response modality.
The present study used a typing-based format (which was similar in approach to that of Lescht et al., 2022) instead of naming responses.
text.formatted: The present study used a typing-based format (which was similar in approach to that of <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Lescht et al., 2022)</ref> instead of naming responses.

text.text: Critically, our use of a typing response modality may have disrupted the internal monitoring systems and auditory feedback loops that AWS use to stabilise speech production (Civier et Running head: Verbal fluency dyslexia and stuttering al., 2010; Postma & Kolk, 1993).
text.formatted: Critically, our use of a typing response modality may have disrupted the internal monitoring systems and auditory feedback loops that AWS use to stabilise speech production <ref type="bibr">(Civier et</ref> Running head: Verbal fluency dyslexia and stuttering <ref type="bibr">al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b113">Postma & Kolk, 1993)</ref>.

text.text: As a result, we may have unmasked a degraded phonological representation that is typically compensated for during speech.
This would explain the reduced cluster sizes observed in the current study.
Without the reinforcement of the auditory loop, the ability to 'group' sounds together effectively is compromised.
In contrast, the self-reported AWS showed lower scores in switching than the neurotypical adults, but not the self-reported dyslexic adults.
For the self-reported AWS, switching may represent a lifelong executive control habit.
Adults who stutter frequently use circumlocution, wherein they switch between target words to avoid feared sounds and maintain perceived fluency (Tichenor & Yaruss, 2019).
text.formatted: Adults who stutter frequently use circumlocution, wherein they switch between target words to avoid feared sounds and maintain perceived fluency <ref type="bibr" target="#b144">(Tichenor & Yaruss, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The lower switching scores observed in our study likely reflect a fundamental, persistent, and modality-free executive search constraint.

While average clustering measures require careful interpretation due to their sensitive nature (Henry et al., 2015; Smith-Spark et al., 2017), the current study's robust sample size provides the necessary power to identify these subtle differences in phonological persistence manifested by the the two neurodivergent groups.
text.formatted: While average clustering measures require careful interpretation due to their sensitive nature <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Henry et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b133">Smith-Spark et al., 2017)</ref>, the current study's robust sample size provides the necessary power to identify these subtle differences in phonological persistence manifested by the the two neurodivergent groups.

text.text: The reduced total word production in both the self-reported dyslexic adults and the selfreported AWS suggests that when a task makes explicit demands on phonological processing, sound-based representations are less accessible than they are in neurotypical adults.
However, a critical divergence between self-reported dyslexic adults and the self-reported AWS appears in the implicit access measured by clustering.
The self-reported dyslexic adults produced cluster sizes comparable to neurotypical controls.
This finding suggests that their underlying phonological representations remain intact and are accessible through automatic, implicit pathways when the conscious processing load is minimized.
For the self-reported dyslexic group, this pattern aligns directly with the access to the phonological representation hypothesis (Boets et al., 2013).
text.formatted: For the self-reported dyslexic group, this pattern aligns directly with the access to the phonological representation hypothesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Boets et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: The phonemic fluency difficulty appears to be localized to the explicit retrieval mechanisms that interface with lexical selection.
In contrast, the self-reported AWS profile reflects a more pervasive difficulty in phonological processing.

Because the selfreported AWS group demonstrated significantly reduced clustering in phonemic fluency compared with both neurotypical and self-reported dyslexic peers, the findings indicate a Running head: Verbal fluency dyslexia and stuttering breakdown in both explicit and implicit access to their phonological representations.

For the self-reported AWS, the difficulty may not be merely one of effortful retrieval but may result from a fundamental instability in the automatic activation of phonologically related neighbors within the onset of the words.

Consequently, while the self-reported dyslexic adults' verbal fluency difficulty may be characterized as a 'retrieval bottleneck,' the self-reported AWSrelated phonemic fluency profile aligns more closely with the phonological representation hypothesis (Ziegler & Goswami, 2005), arising from a global challenge in phonological momentum, with this affecting the system's ability to maintain automatic activation within the phonological network during task performance.
text.formatted: Consequently, while the self-reported dyslexic adults' verbal fluency difficulty may be characterized as a 'retrieval bottleneck,' the self-reported AWSrelated phonemic fluency profile aligns more closely with the phonological representation hypothesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b161">(Ziegler & Goswami, 2005)</ref>, arising from a global challenge in phonological momentum, with this affecting the system's ability to maintain automatic activation within the phonological network during task performance.

text.text: Our findings as they relate to stuttering, therefore, raise several issues relating to the theoretical distinction between an imprecise phonological representation (an encoding/planning challenge) and an intact phonological representation that is difficult to translate, select, or initiate into a motor program.
Within neurocomputational frameworks of speech production, such as GODIVA (Bohland et al., 2010) and DIVA (Guenther et al., 2006), these two processes are anatomically and functionally distinct.

text.text: According to these models, phonological frame selection and sequence planning reside in the left posterior inferior frontal sulcus (pIFS), whereas motor programs are represented in the Speech Sound Map within the ventral premotor cortex (vPMC) and are gated for initiation via basal ganglia-thalamocortical loops (preSMA/SMA (e.g., Bohland et al., 2010; Guenther et al., 2006).
text.formatted: According to these models, phonological frame selection and sequence planning reside in the left posterior inferior frontal sulcus (pIFS), whereas motor programs are represented in the Speech Sound Map within the ventral premotor cortex (vPMC) and are gated for initiation via basal ganglia-thalamocortical loops (preSMA/SMA (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Bohland et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Guenther et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Standard models of stuttering (e.g., Bohland et al., 2010; Guenther et al., 2006) typically attribute dysfluencies to intact phonological representations paired with impaired timing, faulty feedforward control, or elevated basal ganglia initiation thresholds.
text.formatted: Standard models of stuttering (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Bohland et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Guenther et al., 2006)</ref> typically attribute dysfluencies to intact phonological representations paired with impaired timing, faulty feedforward control, or elevated basal ganglia initiation thresholds.

text.text: In contrast, our data point toward lower phonological precision upstream in pIFS.
When phonological codes in pIFS lack distinct sharpness, the feedforward activation signals targeting vPMC motor programs are likely to become ambiguous.

Consequently, the basal ganglia premotor loops responsible for gating motor initiation must operate under heightened uncertainty, thereby increasing competition among candidate motor programs and delaying initiation thresholds.
Crucially, an imprecise phonological representation does not preclude motor-level initiation deficits; rather, it introduces upstream noise into downstream translation.

This proposed mechanism directly bridges linguistic planning and motor execution, aligning with the EXPLAN model of stuttering (Howell & Au-Yeung, 2002), in which dysfluencies arise when delayed linguistic planning (PLAN) fails to deliver a timely, fully specified structure to motor execution (EX).

text.text: The current study used a typing paradigm.
As a consequence of this design decision, questions may arise as to how responding in this modality applies to the language-related challenges experienced by AWS.
The typed response modality may reflect covert articulation (i.e., a subvocal motor planning constraint; van Thorre & Vannuscorps, 2026).
text.formatted: The typed response modality may reflect covert articulation (i.e., a subvocal motor planning constraint; <ref type="bibr" target="#b151">van Thorre & Vannuscorps, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: During written language production, adults who do not stutter engage in internal speech-motor simulation and silent subvocal rehearsal to support phonological working memory and sequence verification (Baddeley, 2003; Postma & Kolk, 1993).
text.formatted: During written language production, adults who do not stutter engage in internal speech-motor simulation and silent subvocal rehearsal to support phonological working memory and sequence verification <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Baddeley, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b113">Postma & Kolk, 1993)</ref>.

text.text: According to such internal feedforward models, the internal feedforward models simulate motor commands prior to overt execution.
If AWS experience difficulties translating phonological representations into timed motor plans, then this constraint may also be found during covert, internal speech simulation.
Consequently, typing bypasses overt vocalisation by reducing blocks, but it does not remove the covert motor assembly component.
If subvocal planning follows a different computational routine, the automatic activation and clustering of phonologically related items may reflect unique network dynamics.
However, we acknowledge that our typing paradigm clearly cannot capture covert vocal tract kinematics.

Future research would require a co-registration of highdensity electroencephalography and electromyography to determine whether covert speechmotor simulation explains latency peaks during typed production.
Semantic fluency was assessed using a single category, while category switching was evaluated via a dual-category task.

Consistent with previous research on both dyslexia (Mengsidiou et al., 2020; Smith-Spark et al., 2017) and stuttering (Bahrami et al., 2014; Gkalitsiou & Werle, 2026), no significant group differences were found in total semantic output or between-category switching.
text.formatted: Consistent with previous research on both dyslexia <ref type="bibr">(Mengsidiou et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b133">Smith-Spark et al., 2017)</ref> and stuttering <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Bahrami et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Gkalitsiou & Werle, 2026)</ref>, no significant group differences were found in total semantic output or between-category switching.

text.text: However, a significant participant group-related divergence emerged in the internal dynamics associated with performance.

While all the participant groups engaged in both within-category and between-category shifts, both the self-reported Running head: Verbal fluency dyslexia and stuttering dyslexic adults and the self-reported AWS demonstrated a disproportionate reduction in within-category switches but similar between-category switches relative to their neurotypical peers.

This finding aligns with patterns previously reported in dyslexia (Mengsidiou et al., 2020), but also it extends the current understanding of AWS by statistically demonstrating in self-reported AWS a trend previously noted in the literature (Gkalitsiou & Werle, 2026).
text.formatted: This finding aligns with patterns previously reported in dyslexia (Mengsidiou et al., <ref type="formula">2020</ref>), but also it extends the current understanding of AWS by statistically demonstrating in self-reported AWS a trend previously noted in the literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Gkalitsiou & Werle, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Crucially, this pattern indicates that the linguistic difficulties experienced by these populations is not characterized by a general executive failure to shift mental sets, but rather by a specific selection and competition difficulty occurring within closely related linguistic representations.
For design fluency, the three participant groups generated similar numbers of unique designs with similar numbers of errors.
Similarly, category-switching performance did not differ across the neurotypical adults, the self-reported adults with dyslexia, and the self-reported AWS (e.g., Bertola et al., 2014; Troyer, 2000).
text.formatted: Similarly, category-switching performance did not differ across the neurotypical adults, the self-reported adults with dyslexia, and the self-reported AWS (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Bertola et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b148">Troyer, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: These findings indicate that the executive fluency difficulties in dyslexia and stuttering are specific to phonologically-and semantically-mediated processing instead of a domain-general challenge in processing speed or executive control.

Although executive fluency paradigms carry inherent task-impurity problems (e.g., Anderle & Venuti, 2026), the use of an equivalent non-verbal baseline measure demonstrates that the executive "machinery" for initiation, flexibility, and switching remains intact in both neurodivergent groups.
text.formatted: Although executive fluency paradigms carry inherent task-impurity problems (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Anderle & Venuti, 2026)</ref>, the use of an equivalent non-verbal baseline measure demonstrates that the executive "machinery" for initiation, flexibility, and switching remains intact in both neurodivergent groups.

text.text: While the current study, therefore, provides important and novel insights into the cognitivelinguistic profiles of the self-reported AWS and the self-reported dyslexic adults, several design limitations must be acknowledged.
Our modification of the verbal fluency tasks from an oral to a typed response format introduced a distinct methodological trade-off.

On the one hand, typing effectively isolates cognitivelinguistic retrieval by bypassing oral-motor execution constraints, physical speech blocks, and social-evaluative anxiety, while simultaneously facilitating large-scale web-based administration.
On the other hand, this same modification introduces task-demand asymmetries across the two neurodivergent profiles.

For the self-reported AWS, typed administration decouples phonological retrieval from speech-motor planning and execution, a core interface in spoken disfluency frameworks (e.g., DIVA/GODIVA models; Bohland et al., 2010; Guenther et al., 2006).
text.formatted: For the self-reported AWS, typed administration decouples phonological retrieval from speech-motor planning and execution, a core interface in spoken disfluency frameworks (e.g., DIVA/GODIVA models; <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Bohland et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Guenther et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, for the self-reported dyslexic adults, typing imposes additional orthographic assembly and fine-motor planning demands (Košir et al., 2024; Sumner et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Conversely, for the self-reported dyslexic adults, typing imposes additional orthographic assembly and fine-motor planning demands <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Košir et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b141">Sumner et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Because cognitive resources have to be shared between spelling verification and lexical search (Sumner et al., 2012), inter-response latencies can become inflated.
text.formatted: Because cognitive resources have to be shared between spelling verification and lexical search <ref type="bibr" target="#b141">(Sumner et al., 2012)</ref>, inter-response latencies can become inflated.

text.text: Consequently, it is crucial to dissociate general processing or typing execution speed from underlying linguistic retrieval.
Despite these manual sequencing demands, several lines of evidence indicate that they do not systematically bias our results.
First, because manual requirements are balanced across participant groups, any generalized motor difficulties in AWS would have suppressed performance uniformly across all the tasks.
Instead, group differences were task-specific: they were evident in phonemic fluency, but absent in semantic fluency, switching responses, and design fluency.
This pattern confirms that the observed effects reflect specific cognitive phonological constraints rather than general motor or output limitations.
However, it should be noted that evidence regarding general manual sequencing deficits in AWS remains equivocal (Cross & Luper, 1983; Olander et al., 2010; Zelaznik et al., 1997).
text.formatted: However, it should be noted that evidence regarding general manual sequencing deficits in AWS remains equivocal <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Cross & Luper, 1983;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b100">Olander et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b160">Zelaznik et al., 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Second, concerns regarding an orthographic bottle in dyslexia are affected by procedural controls and qualitative errors are mitigated against by the instructions given to the participants and the nature of their error responses.

The participants received explicit instructions to ignore typographical errors, scoring accommodated phonologically plausible spellings, and produced errors that were predominantly morphological substitutions and repetitions (e.g., "fly, flying, flew") instead of the surface-level orthographic breakdowns typical of dyslexia (Afonso et al., 2022; Connelly et al., 2006; Elsherif et al., 2025).

text.text: This points to a deeper lexical selection challenge that persists even when oral output channels are bypassed.
While individual typing proficiency and hardware latency were not explicitly measured, our moderate sample size (N = 62 per group) effectively distributed this variance across conditions.
Nevertheless, future research using a similar paradigm should incorporate a standardized baseline typing assessment as a covariate.
More broadly, our adoption of a typed paradigm highlights the trade-off between specialized, in person laboratory studies and well-powered remote paradigms.

By leveraging remote administration via Prolific and online communication, our study recruited a moderate-powered sample (N = 62 per group) that significantly exceeded those reported in previous work (e.g., Gkalitsiou et al., 2018, N = 32 AWS; Smith-Spark et al., 2017, N = 28 dyslexia).

text.text: This larger sample size directly addresses recent replicability concerns raised by Leung et al. (2026) and van Bergen et al. (2026) regarding the reliability of the findings obtained in the study of dyslexia and related language neurodivergences.

text.text: Coupled with strict group matching on age, gender, print exposure, and IQ, the current sample provides a stable foundation for our findings, even though the exclusion of spoken output naturally limits direct generalizability to real-world oral communication.
Future work combining synchronized eye-tracking or keystroke logging could focus on orthographic planning latencies that underlies lexical-phonological search mechanics.
There are also limitations which relate to participant recruitment and diagnostic classification that must also be acknowledged.

The dyslexia cohort was recruited based on self-reported formal diagnoses without the participants having to state the nature or extent of previous phonics-based interventions, which can influence task performance in phonological processing tasks (e.g., elision; Elbro & Petersen, 2004).

text.text: While remote testing precludes inperson clinical validation, group allocation was controlled using validated screening instruments, which provide reliable, highly specific classifications of lifelong neurodivergent traits (Feng et al., 2021; Garvin & Krishnan, 2021; Pennington & LeFly, 2001) in the context of the financial and systemic barriers restricting adult clinical re-evaluation (Ahuvia et al., 2026).

text.text: Although our primary analyses treated groups categorically, our behavioural data (see the supplementary materials) revealed an overlap: 96.8% of self-reported AWS scored in the mild dyslexia range on the standardized screeners, alongside a high prevalence of selfreported childhood stuttering among the self-reported adult dyslexics.
Instead of undermining the group classifications, this surface-level overlap emphasises the need for transdiagnostic frameworks.

Moving beyond binary clinical labels, dimensional and latent-variable approaches Running head: Verbal fluency dyslexia and stuttering (e.g., structural equation modelling) would seem to be essential to mapping out how interacting cognitive dimensions predict executive fluency outcomes across different neurodivergent profiles.
Finally, potential domain-general confounds were carefully controlled through our task battery design.

To avoid the lexical access confounds inherent to linguistically based executive tasks like the Stroop task (Elsherif et al., 2025; Stroop, 1935), we used a non-verbal design fluency task to isolate domain-general executive function and found that there were no neurodivergence-related effects.

text.text: Furthermore potential concerns regarding earlier cognitive fatigue in neurodivergent populations (Nicolson & Fawcett, 1990; Starkweather & Gottwald, 1990) are mitigated by our fixed-task order.
text.formatted: Furthermore potential concerns regarding earlier cognitive fatigue in neurodivergent populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">(Nicolson & Fawcett, 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b138">Starkweather & Gottwald, 1990</ref>) are mitigated by our fixed-task order.

text.text: Core cognitive-linguistic measures are administered early in the testing session, whereas tasks showing comparable performance across groups were positioned at the conclusion where fatigue would most likely exacerbate group differences.

To conclude, our results indicate that, in verbal fluency performance at the very least, dyslexia reflects a challenge to access phonological representations, while stuttering is defined by the phonological representation itself.

These findings advance our understanding of speech-and language-related neurodivergence by demonstrating that, while overlapping phonological processing differences frame a shared cognitive continuum, distinct behavioural outcomes preserve critical diagnostic boundaries.
This explanatory framework reconciles how these two groups share surface-level phonological challenges while operating under different cognitive mechanisms.
Ultimately, we argue that these findings carry profound theoretical and translational weight for how the architecture of neurodivergent cognitive profiles is conceptualized.

At a theoretical level, our results challenge rigid paradigms by demonstrating that developmental stuttering and dyslexia are best understood through a shared, spectrumbased lens characterized by overlapping difficulties in the phonological system.

By isolating these challenges to phonological representation and access, while also ruling out a global executive difficulty, we provide a more precise cognitive map of how linguistic precision constrains fluency across distinct neurodivergent populations.
From an applied perspective, Running head: Verbal fluency dyslexia and stuttering we feel that these insights should shift clinical and educational paradigms in relation to neurodivergence.

Rather than treating reading challenges and speech difficulties in absolute isolation, we argue that clinicians, educators, and speech-language therapists should recognize their shared phonological roots.

Interventions targeted at strengthening phonological precision and managing lexical competition could yield downstream benefits for both literacy acquisition and speech fluency, offering a unified, cross-diagnostic framework that better serves the complex needs of neurodivergent adults.

Overall, the hierarchical regression analyses showed different predictors across executive fluency tasks.
Non-verbal intelligence served as a baseline predictor of core output volume and switching frequency (Step 1).

Introducing language-specific predictors demonstrated that phonological and lexical precision uniquely drove output volume and switching accuracy in verbal fluency contexts but played no predictive role in design fluency (Step 2).

Finally, neurodivergent status showed clear behavioral differences (Step 3): while dyslexia selectively predicted more words per cluster and fewer switches during phonemic fluency, stuttering exerted a broader impact across both explicit output and implicit clustering measures.

Neither neurodivergent profile predicted non-verbal design fluency, confirming that executive fluency constraints are domain-specific to linguistic processing rather than reflecting generalized executive function difficulties.
